package com.clockwork.core; /** * Notified of everything the controller does. * *

Every method has an empty default so a listener only implements the * events it cares about. Callbacks arrive on whichever thread called the * controller, so a Swing listener is responsible for its own hop to the event * dispatch thread. */ public interface RoutineListener { /** * A routine was created, deleted, renamed or reconfigured, or the whole list * was replaced. The whole view should be rebuilt, and so should the whole * saved state. * *

One clock's runs changing arrives as * {@link #onHistoryChanged(Routine)} instead. Every clock's runs being * cleared at once arrives here, because at that point all of it did move. */ default void onRoutinesChanged() { } default void onRunStarted(Routine routine) { } default void onLapTaken(Routine routine, Lap lap) { } /** * A run ended and was written to history, either because the user stopped * it or because it was auto-abandoned. Check {@link Run#getStatus()}. */ default void onRunFinished(Routine routine, Run run) { } /** * One clock's recorded runs changed and nothing else did, which is what a * finished run and a cleared clock both are. * *

Separate from {@link #onRoutinesChanged()} because the saved state that * has to be rewritten is that one clock's runs rather than every clock's * settings and every clock's runs. Rewriting all of it on the event that * happens most often is exactly what the storage layout exists to avoid, so * this is the announcement that says how little moved. * *

Like the rebuild announcement it means the view is out of date, so a * listener that draws should redraw. */ default void onHistoryChanged(Routine routine) { } /** * A run in progress was thrown away and recorded nothing. */ default void onRunCancelled(Routine routine) { } /** * A countdown crossed one of the last three second boundaries before zero, * with {@code secondsLeft} at three, two, or one. Each of the three fires * once per run at most. * *

Countdowns only, since a clock counting up has no known end to count in * to. A run that is paused crosses nothing, because its remaining time is * held still while it waits, so a countdown that pauses at two and a half * seconds still has its two and its one ahead of it when it resumes. * *

Only the boundaries a run really has. A countdown started with less * than three seconds on it gets the beats that fit and no more, and one * started with less than a second gets none, so nothing is ever counted in * for a moment that had already passed when the run began. * *

A tick that arrives late crosses more than one boundary at once and * still announces one, for the second the countdown is actually in, rather * than firing the ones it slept through in a burst. * * @param routine the clock counting down * @param secondsLeft whole seconds left on it, three, two, or one */ default void onCountInSecond(Routine routine, int secondsLeft) { } /** * A countdown reached zero and the run carried on into overtime. This is * the only moment worth alerting on and it fires once per run. * *

A routine with {@link Routine#isStopAtZero()} set never sees this. * Its run ends at zero instead, so the moment arrives as * {@link #onRunFinished(Routine, Run)} and there is exactly one thing to * alert on either way. */ default void onCountdownExpired(Routine routine) { } }

package com.clockwork.ui; /** * The designated hotkey target, as the side panel sees it. * *

The panel needs to show which clock the keys act on and to let the user * change it, but it is not the owner of that fact. The plugin is, because the * designation is persisted and is read by the hotkey handlers whether the panel * is open or shut. So the panel is handed this instead of a field of its own, * and there is one copy of the answer. * *

Both methods are called on the event dispatch thread, which is where the * cards live and where the plugin does its own reads. */ public interface HotkeyTargetHandle { /** * The designated clock, or null when there is none. */ String getHotkeyTargetId(); /** * Designates a clock, or clears the designation when given null. * *

The implementation is expected to persist it and to redraw whatever is * showing it, so the caller does not have to. */ void setHotkeyTargetId(String routineId); }
